alternatives.concept: Combine Earth and climate science, soils, water and biodiversity with economics, quantitative methods and sustainability governance. Geological and laboratory fieldwork, GIS and spatial projects connect physical evidence with adaptation and energy decisions; dedicated environmental economics, advanced sustainability data science and the individual VU thesis remain important gaps.

alternatives.labelRationale: The schedule spans Earth science, water, climate, resources, economics, spatial data and policy; the title describes its actual interdisciplinary core.

alternatives.concept: Connect Earth-resource science with energy-system analysis, renewable design, resource recovery and life-cycle assessment. Five economics courses add 37.5 EC of theory, public-policy analysis and econometrics, giving this direction greater economic and technical energy weight than the integrated water, risk and biodiversity programme.

alternatives.labelRationale: Actual resource,energy-conversion/design,life-cycle,circular-recovery andfiveeconomiccourses substantiate the title; generic economics is not renamed a specialist environmental-economics course.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Four courses (30 EC) differ in each direction. The integrated programme emphasises hazards, nature-based infrastructure, biodiversity and delta water management. This direction instead adds macroeconomics, public economics, life-cycle assessment and renewable-system design. All differences are substantive consequences of economic evaluation and resource/energy focus, not numerical substitutions.

alternatives.concept: Combine Earth systems, water and delta systems, geospatial analysis and physical environmental investigation with programming, algorithms, machine learning and neural prediction. The computational courses supply general methods for environmental questions supported by the science courses; particular environmental project topics are not guaranteed, and specialist environmental economics, ethics and the VU thesis remain gaps.

alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Five courses (37.5 EC) differ from the closest and seven (52.5 EC) from the resource/economic programme. Programming, algorithms, machine learning, neural networks and Earth-system modelling replace biodiversity, nature-based infrastructure, renewable-energy analysis, microeconomics and governance relative to the closest. These choices shift the organising priority to computational environmental inquiry, not cosmetic substitutions.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both address global climatic change; UCR emphasizes anthropogenic climate impacts.
Both introduce interacting Earth systems and field observation.

Both model interacting Earth systems and environmental change. UCR also studies climate proxies and tracers; its description does not establish the complete VU Python, land-use and agent-based modelling sequence.
Both investigate soils, hydrology and the landscape through field/lab methods.
Delta water-management cases do not establish the VU physical hydrology and quantitative flow-process sequence.
Both train in GIS and Earth-observation datasets.
Both analyse natural hazards and risk reduction.
VU has a specified first-year climate-adaptation field course; related UCR field activities are not the same credited placement.
VU requires its own specified 6-EC spatial-solutions fieldwork; UCR delta research and field activities are related, not an exact equivalent.
No single retained course is judged a sufficiently direct counterpart; related project, social or ecological contributions do not replace this specified requirement.
Both study energy transition and renewable supply; UCR includes quantitative resource and system analysis, without claiming identical breadth.
Both examine energy and Earth resources; UCR focuses on geoscience research.
Biological diversity foundations do not establish the VU nature-management course.

notes.text: These UCR programmes combine substantial Earth and sustainability study with different economic or computational priorities. They do not reproduce dedicated environmental economics, physical hydrology and nature-management depth, environmental ethics, VU’s two specified fieldwork units or its required individual 12-EC thesis. Data and machine-learning courses supply general methods alongside environmental science, rather than the same sustainability Big Data course. Optional independent research requires approval and is outside the 24-course schedules; it does not replace the VU thesis.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Earth Sciences, Economics and Sustainability connects physical Earth systems with economic choices and spatial sustainability problems. Students study climate risk, water, land, energy and resources using field research, data analysis and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers an integrated Earth, water, risk and biodiversity programme, a resource and energy programme with greater economic evaluation, and a computational direction combining environmental science with programming and machine learning. Spatial analysis, laboratory and field activities support these related responses. Dedicated environmental economics, advanced sustainability-specific data science, environmental ethics, VU’s specified fieldwork and the individual thesis remain important differences. Computational courses provide general methods; particular environmental project topics are not guaranteed.

curriculum.routeLabel: Ordinary full-time bachelor; Urban Challenges restricted elective
curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC comprises 144 EC of required courses, one 6 EC restricted choice and 30 EC of free study. Fieldwork preparation requires 24 eligible first-year EC; second-year fieldwork requires 60 EC including the first fieldwork. Thesis entry requires 126 EC including recognised fieldwork. Free-choice courses have level and approval rules. The first-year study-advice norm is 42 EC. A language test or remediation gates the Soil and Landscape grade; mentoring and Geoflex obligations carry no credits.
